THOUGHT: This 57-year-old obese, current smoker presents with fever, chills, headache, right-sided pleuritic chest pain (worsening on inspiration), and a new productive cough — all beginning three days after open cholecystectomy. The physical exam reveals inspiratory crackles at the right lung base, and the chest X-ray shows right lower lobe infiltrates. Laboratory findings include leukocytosis. These findings are highly consistent with a pulmonary infection. Postoperative pneumonia is a common complication, especially in patients with risk factors including advanced age, obesity, smoking (17 pack-years), and recent major abdominal surgery — all of which impair respiratory mechanics (e.g., splinting, reduced diaphragmatic excursion), mucociliary clearance, and immune surveillance. Pleuritic chest pain and inspiratory crackles suggest involvement of the pleura and alveolar consolidation, respectively. While other postoperative complications such as pulmonary embolism or atelectasis must be considered, PE typically presents with dyspnea, tachypnea, and often hypoxia — none of which are reported here; moreover, PE does not cause productive cough, fever, leukocytosis, or infiltrates on CXR. Atelectasis may cause low-grade fever and mild respiratory symptoms but rarely causes high fever (39°C), productive cough, or focal infiltrates with crackles. Early empyema or lung abscess are less likely without more indolent course or cavitary changes on imaging. Given the acute onset, systemic signs (fever, chills, leukocytosis), respiratory symptoms, and radiographic consolidation, the most likely diagnosis is hospital-acquired (or postoperative) pneumonia — specifically, right lower lobe pneumonia.

DIAGNOSIS: Hospital-acquired pneumonia
